name: logo-wall
description: A grid of customer, partner, or funder logos as social proof.
purpose: Use for the credibility slide — the 'trusted by' / 'our funders' / 'participating agencies' wall. Marks render as token-colored silhouettes (a CSS mask filled with `var(--logo-ink)`), so the wall is one cohesive texture that re-tones per theme and color-mode and stays AA on any ground; the `color` variant gives each mark its own categorical palette hue.

eyebrow.description: Optional kicker above the headline — wrap a short label in backticks, e.g. `Trusted by`.

title.description: Optional headline above the wall. A claim earns its place (‘400+ teams run board prep on Lattice’); a bare label (‘Customers’) does not.

logos.description: One list item per mark, authored as `- ![Brand name](brand.svg)`. The alt text is the accessible label, not a rendered caption. SVG is preferred so marks stay crisp at projector scale. To try the layout before you have the marks, use Lattice's sample logos: `![Acme](sample:logo-acme.svg)` (the full set is in `lib/samples/README.md`).

caption.description: Optional name + pill stacked below a mark, centered. Nest a list under the image: plain text is the name, a `{…}` token in backticks (`{Series B}`) is the pill. Either or both, per mark.

whenToUse.title: The proof is the logos
whenToUse.body: Customers, partners, funders, accreditations, participating agencies — anywhere a set of recognizable marks carries more weight than a sentence. The audience scans the wall and concludes 'serious company keeps this company.'

whenToUse.title: Marks read as one texture
whenToUse.body: Every mark is filled with the same palette token, so a loud red logo can't outshout a quiet one — the wall reads as a single credential, not a ransom note of competing brand colors. Because the fill is a token, it re-tones for theme + dark mode and stays AA on any ground.

whenToUse.title: Eight to eighteen marks
whenToUse.body: Enough to signal breadth, few enough that each is legible. Fewer than six looks thin; past eighteen the marks shrink below recognition — curate to the most recognizable names or split across two slides.

whenToUse.title: Marks of mixed shapes
whenToUse.body: Marks share one area, kept between the smallest and largest of their old areas, and no mark stands taller than the old row: beside a 1:2 crest, wordmarks come down to a square badge's area and the crest keeps its own, 2× apart (a 4:1 wordmark used to get 2.7× the crest's area, a 3:1 wordmark 3.6×). A wall that fit before still fits; rows are balanced and centered (ten marks break 4/3/3). A wall of one shape keeps its old size. The wall sizes from SVG marks (a local file, `sample:` or a `data:` SVG); a raster or remote mark keeps the equal-cell grid. Demo deck: `examples/logo-wall-equal-weight.md`.

antiPatterns.title: Names that need a sentence
antiPatterns.body: If each entity needs a role, a quote, or a metric beside it, this is the wrong layout. Use `actors` (who owns what), `cards-grid` (a short body per item), or `quote` (a single testimonial).

antiPatterns.title: Logos nobody recognizes
antiPatterns.body: A wall of unknown marks proves nothing and asks the audience to squint. If the names don't carry on sight, state the count as a `big-number` ('400+ teams') instead.

antiPatterns.title: Mismatched raster art
antiPatterns.body: The mark is rendered as a silhouette (a CSS mask / inline SVG), so it must be clean vector with real transparency — a raster PNG or a logo whose negative space is a white fill won't read. Source SVG marks drawn as filled shapes; color is supplied by the palette token, not the file.

related.name: actors
related.when: each named entity owns a responsibility, not just lends its logo

related.name: cards-grid
related.when: each item needs a line of body text, not just a mark

related.name: big-number
related.when: the proof is a count ('400+ teams'), not the individual marks

related.name: quote
related.when: one customer's testimonial carries the slide

related.name: image
related.when: a single visual, not a grid of marks, is the evidence

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing a caption's pill as plain nested text instead of `{…}` in backticks.
commonMistakes.fix: Under a mark's nested caption list, plain text becomes the NAME line; only a `{…}` token in backticks (e.g. `` `{Series B}` ``) becomes the pill — writing the round label without backticks renders it as a second name line instead of a pill.

commonMistakes.mistake: Placing the eyebrow paragraph after the headline instead of before it.
commonMistakes.fix: The eyebrow matches `p > code:only-child` as the section's kicker, positioned before the `## headline` — placed after, the masthead lift re-seats it as the italic, secondary-color subtitle instead of the intended mono kicker.

commonMistakes.mistake: An SVG mark whose viewBox carries empty margin around the logo.
commonMistakes.fix: Equal weight is measured on the mark's box, not its ink, so the margin counts as mark and the logo draws smaller than its neighbors. Crop each SVG's `viewBox` to its ink.

commonMistakes.mistake: Packing more marks than the slide can hold at a readable size.
commonMistakes.fix: A wall that would fit only with marks too small to read keeps the equal-cell grid, and the export flags its overflow. Split the roster across two slides, or drop the captions.

variantDecisionRule.useWhen: The default token-recolored silhouette treatment — one cohesive texture, theme-safe.
The individual brand colors are themselves part of the credibility signal — a recognizable, colorful set of household names worth preserving.
The roster is long (12-18+ marks) and captions aren't needed — packs more columns, captions off.
